questions.question: A student releases a sphere at the top of a cylinder of washing-up liquid and uses a stopwatch and metre rule. Describe a method to determine an accurate value of the terminal velocity of the sphere.
questions.answer: Mark two points well below the surface, measure the distance between them with a metre rule, time the fall between them with a stopwatch, use v = distance / time, and repeat and average.
steps: Release the sphere at the top and wait until it has reached terminal velocity, so the timed section is at constant speed.
Mark two points (e.g. rubber bands) well below the surface and measure the distance d between them with a metre rule.
Use a stopwatch to time the sphere from the upper to the lower mark, starting and stopping when the bottom of the sphere passes each mark.
Calculate v = d / t; repeat several times and take the mean to reduce random error.
Check the sphere is at terminal velocity by timing two equal sections; equal times confirm constant speed.

questions.question: Explain why using a larger sphere would increase the percentage uncertainty in the calculated terminal velocity.
questions.answer: A larger sphere falls faster, so the time over the fixed distance is shorter and the reaction-time error is a larger fraction; its diameter also makes the position of the marks less precise.
steps: A larger sphere has a greater terminal velocity (v is proportional to r^2), so it takes less time to fall the measured distance.
The uncertainty in starting and stopping the stopwatch (reaction time) is roughly constant, so it is a larger percentage of the shorter time.
The diameter of the sphere is larger, so the position at which it passes each mark is less precise.
The uncertainty in the distance is a larger fraction of the measured distance, so the percentage uncertainty in v = d / t increases.

questions.question: Complete the free-body force diagram for the sphere travelling at terminal velocity.
questions.answer: Weight acts downwards; upthrust and viscous drag both act upwards, and their sum equals the weight.
steps: Weight acts vertically downwards from the centre of the sphere.
Upthrust acts vertically upwards (from the displaced liquid).
Viscous drag acts vertically upwards, opposing the motion.
At terminal velocity the resultant is zero, so weight = upthrust + viscous drag.

questions.question: The terminal velocity is 0.16 m s-1. Given radius 4.8 x 10^-3 m, weight 3.5 x 10^-2 N and liquid density 1.1 x 10^3 kg m-3, calculate the viscosity of the washing-up liquid in Pa s.
questions.answer: Viscosity = 2.1 Pa s.
steps: At terminal velocity weight = upthrust + drag, so the Stokes drag F = 3.5 x 10^-2 - 5.0 x 10^-3 = 3.0 x 10^-2 N.
Stokes' law: F = 6 pi eta r v, so eta = F / (6 pi r v).

questions.question: Explain why the top rubber band should be placed a short distance below the surface of the oil.
questions.answer: The sphere accelerates from rest when it enters the oil, so it needs a short distance to reach terminal velocity before the timed section starts.
steps: When the sphere enters the oil it starts from rest and accelerates.
It takes a short distance for the drag to balance the weight and upthrust (terminal velocity).
Placing the top band below the surface ensures the timed section is at constant terminal velocity.

questions.question: Discuss the benefit of adding a third rubber band halfway between the top and bottom bands.
questions.answer: With three bands the two sections can be timed separately; equal times for each section show the sphere is at constant terminal velocity, and the two results can be averaged to reduce random error.
steps: The middle band gives two timed sections: top to middle, and middle to bottom.
If both sections take the same time, the sphere is moving at a constant (terminal) velocity.
Two independent timings can be averaged, which reduces random error.

questions.question: Which quantity is represented by the first symbol in the equation for viscosity? The symbol is not legible in the extracted text.
questions.answer: The weight of the sphere
steps: (4/3) pi r^3 is the volume of the sphere.
Volume x density of the sphere (rho_s) gives its mass, and multiplying by g gives its weight.
So (4/3) pi r^3 rho_s g is the weight of the sphere, acting downwards.

questions.question: Which quantity is represented by the second symbol in the viscosity equation? The symbol is not legible in the extracted text.
questions.answer: The upthrust on the sphere (the weight of oil it displaces)
steps: (4/3) pi r^3 is the volume of oil displaced by the fully submerged sphere.
Multiplying by the oil density rho_o and g gives the weight of oil displaced.
By Archimedes principle this is the upthrust on the sphere, acting upwards.

questions.question: Which quantity is represented by the expression 6 pi r v in the viscosity equation? The symbol is not legible in the extracted text.
questions.answer: The viscous drag force on the sphere (Stokes drag)
steps: 6 pi r eta v is Stokes' law for the drag force on a small sphere moving through a viscous fluid.
At terminal velocity this upward drag, with the upthrust, balances the weight.
So 6 pi r eta v is the viscous drag acting upwards on the sphere.

questions.question: The accepted viscosity of the oil is 41 mPa s at 24 degrees C, but the student obtained 36 mPa s. Suggest a possible reason for the lower value.
questions.answer: The oil was warmer than 24 degrees C (viscosity falls as temperature rises), or the fall times were measured too short.
steps: Viscosity decreases as temperature increases.
If the oil was warmer than 24 degrees C, its viscosity would be lower than the accepted value.
Alternatively, a shorter measured time would give a higher terminal velocity and so a lower calculated viscosity.

keywords: points V W X Y Z
questions.question: A student releases a ball bearing at point V and times its fall through a measured distance in oil. Which two points should he use? A V and Y; B W and Y; C X and Y; D W and Z. The diagram with the points is not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: C: X and Y
steps: The timed distance must be one where the ball moves at terminal velocity, so that distance / time gives a constant velocity.
V and W are in the air or at the surface, where the ball is not in the oil or is still accelerating after entering the oil; using V or W (options A, B, D) includes this accelerating motion.
X is a short distance below the surface, far enough for the ball to have reached terminal velocity.
Z is at the bottom of the cylinder, where the base can affect the ball, so Y (above Z) is used as the lower point: X and Y, option C.

questions.question: For which conditions does Stokes' law apply? A spherical objects and laminar flow; B spherical objects and low viscosity; C cylindrical objects and laminar flow; D cylindrical objects and low viscosity.
questions.answer: A - spherical objects and laminar flow.
steps: Stokes' law applies to small spheres moving through a fluid.
The flow around the sphere must be laminar (streamlined).
Low viscosity and cylindrical objects are not conditions of Stokes' law.

questions.question: Explain what is meant by terminal velocity.
questions.answer: The constant maximum velocity reached by a falling object when the resultant force is zero, i.e. drag plus upthrust equals weight.
steps: As the object falls, the viscous drag increases with speed.
The acceleration falls as the resultant force decreases.
When drag plus upthrust equals weight the resultant force is zero, so the object moves at a constant (terminal) velocity.

questions.question: A glass sphere of diameter 35 mm falls at terminal velocity. Density of glass is 2.52 x 10^3 kg m-3 and density of liquid is 1.43 x 10^3 kg m-3. Show that the drag force is about 0.2 N.
questions.answer: Drag = (rho_glass - rho_liquid) V g = 0.24 N, which is about 0.2 N to 1 s.f.
steps: At terminal velocity the drag equals the net weight: F = (rho_glass - rho_liquid) V g.
0.240 N rounds to about 0.2 N to 1 s.f., as required.

questions.question: Deduce from the graph of v against d^2 whether the flow of liquid around the spheres was laminar. The graph is not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: Yes: the graph is a straight line through the origin, so v is proportional to d^2 as Stokes' law (laminar flow) predicts.
steps: Stokes' law, valid for laminar flow, gives v = k d^2, which is a straight line through the origin when v is plotted against d^2.
The points lie close to a single straight best-fit line.
The line passes through the origin (0, 0), so v is directly proportional to d^2.
This agrees with Stokes' law, so the flow was laminar.

questions.question: Using the student's graph of v against d^2 and v = k d^2, determine the value of k. The graph is not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: k = 6.0 m^-1 s^-1 (gradient of the line)
steps: v = k d^2, so k is the gradient of the graph of v against d^2.
Take a large triangle on the line, for example from (0, 0) to (10.0 x 10^-4 m^2, 6.0 x 10^-3 m s^-1).
k = change in v / change in d^2 = 6.0 x 10^-3 / 10.0 x 10^-4 = 6.0 m^-1 s^-1 (accept about 5.8 to 6.2).

questions.question: The constant k is given by k = (rho_glass - rho_liquid) g / (18 eta), where eta is the viscosity of the liquid. Using rho_glass = 2.52 x 10^3 kg m-3 and rho_liquid = 1.43 x 10^3 kg m-3, determine the viscosity eta. (k = 6.0 m-1 s-1 from part (c)(ii).)
questions.answer: eta = 99 Pa s (about 1.0 x 10^2 Pa s), using k = 6.0 m^-1 s^-1
steps: Rearrange the printed formula k = (rho_g - rho_s) g / (18 eta): eta = (rho_g - rho_s) g / (18 k).
Density difference = 2.52 x 10^3 - 1.43 x 10^3 = 1.09 x 10^3 kg m^-3.
eta = 99 Pa s (about 1.0 x 10^2 Pa s).

questions.question: Using a balance and digital calliper, describe how the student could calculate the drag force on the ball when it falls at terminal velocity, given the density of the liquid is known.
questions.answer: Drag = weight - upthrust = (m - rho_liquid V) g, with m from the balance and V = (4/3) pi r^3 from the calliper diameter.
steps: Use the balance to measure the mass m of the ball, so its weight is W = mg.
Use the calliper to measure the diameter d several times; find the radius r = d / 2.
Calculate the volume V = (4/3) pi r^3 of the ball.
Upthrust U = rho_liquid V g, using the known liquid density.
Drag F = W - U = (m - rho_liquid V) g, because at terminal velocity drag = weight - upthrust.

questions.question: The ball falls at terminal velocity 5.4 x 10^-4 m s-1 with radius 0.50 x 10^-2 m and drag force 1.1 x 10^-2 N, with laminar flow. Calculate the viscosity of the liquid.
questions.answer: Viscosity = 216 Pa s (about 2.2 x 10^2 Pa s) from the stated values.
steps: Stokes' law for laminar flow: F = 6 pi eta r v, so eta = F / (6 pi r v).
Denominator: 6 pi x r x v = 6 pi x 0.50 x 10^-2 x 5.4 x 10^-4 = 5.09 x 10^-5 m2 s-1.

questions.question: A sphere falls through a viscous liquid. Which row of the table describes the upthrust and the viscous drag as it accelerates downwards? The table is not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: B: upthrust constant, viscous drag increasing
steps: The sphere is fully submerged, so it displaces a constant volume of liquid and the upthrust (weight of liquid displaced) stays constant.
Viscous drag (6 pi eta r v) increases as the speed v increases while the sphere accelerates.
So upthrust is constant and viscous drag is increasing: row B.

questions.question: State the conditions under which Stokes' law applies to an object moving through a fluid.
questions.answer: The object is spherical and smooth, the flow around it is laminar, the speed is low, and the fluid is large compared with the object (no wall effects).
steps: The object must be a sphere so the drag formula 6 pi eta r v applies.
The flow must be laminar (streamlined), not turbulent, which needs a low speed.
The container must be large compared with the sphere so wall effects are negligible.

questions.question: Explain the shape of the graph obtained by the student for the ball-bearing falling through a liquid. The graph is not in the extracted text.
questions.answer: Gradient (velocity) starts at zero and increases, then becomes constant: the ball accelerates at first, and as the viscous drag rises the acceleration falls to zero, so it falls at constant terminal velocity (a straight line).
steps: At release the ball is at rest, so the gradient of the displacement-time graph (the velocity) is zero at the start.
Its weight is greater than the upthrust, so there is a downward resultant force and the ball accelerates: the graph gets steeper.
As its speed increases the viscous drag increases, so the resultant force and the acceleration decrease, and the gradient increases more and more slowly.
When drag plus upthrust equals weight the resultant force is zero, so the ball moves at constant terminal velocity: the graph is a straight line of constant gradient.

questions.question: The ball-bearing has diameter 1.6 mm and the difference between upthrust and weight is 1.45 x 10^-4 N. Calculate the viscosity, assuming Stokes' law applies. The terminal velocity is needed and is read from the graph.
questions.answer: eta = 0.046 Pa s (about 4.6 x 10^-2 Pa s), using v = 0.21 m s^-1 from the graph
steps: The graph is a straight line from about 0.6 s, so the ball is at terminal velocity: v = gradient = 11.7 cm / (1.15 - 0.60) s = 21 cm s^-1 = 0.21 m s^-1.
At terminal velocity the drag equals the difference between weight and upthrust: F = 1.45 x 10^-4 N.
Stokes' law F = 6 pi eta r v, so eta = F / (6 pi r v) = 1.45 x 10^-4 / (6 pi x 8.0 x 10^-4 x 0.21) = 0.046 Pa s (graph reading, so accept about 0.044 to 0.048).

questions.question: The liquid is heated and the experiment repeated, and the ball bearing takes less time to fall a given distance. Explain why, assuming the density of the liquid is constant.
questions.answer: Heating lowers the viscosity, so the viscous drag at a given speed is smaller; the ball reaches a higher terminal velocity and so covers the distance in less time.
steps: Viscosity of a liquid decreases as its temperature increases.
With a smaller viscosity, the viscous drag 6 pi eta r v is smaller at any given speed.
The ball therefore accelerates for longer and reaches a greater terminal velocity, since v is proportional to 1 / eta.
A higher average speed means the given distance is covered in less time.

questions.question: The graph shows terminal velocity against mass for small spheres of equal diameter in a viscous liquid. Which describes the gradient for a liquid of greater viscosity? A a greater gradient; B a smaller gradient; C a variable gradient; D the same gradient.
questions.answer: B - a smaller gradient.
steps: Terminal velocity v = (mg - upthrust) / (6 pi eta r), so v is linear in mass with gradient g / (6 pi eta r).
The sphere radius is the same, so the gradient is inversely proportional to viscosity eta.
A greater viscosity therefore gives a smaller gradient.

questions.question: A metal sphere is released from rest in oil. Explain why the sphere reaches terminal velocity.
questions.answer: Weight exceeds upthrust at first, so the sphere accelerates; drag increases with speed until drag plus upthrust equals weight, the resultant force is zero and the sphere moves at constant terminal velocity.
steps: At release the speed is zero, so the viscous drag is zero.
Weight is greater than upthrust, so the resultant force is downwards and the sphere accelerates.
As its speed increases, the viscous drag increases, reducing the resultant force and the acceleration.
When drag plus upthrust equals weight the resultant force is zero, so the sphere reaches a constant terminal velocity.

questions.question: The sphere falls 0.45 m at terminal velocity in 7.3 s. Given radius 0.90 x 10^-3 m and oil viscosity 2.1 x 10^-1 Pa s, calculate the viscous drag force, assuming Stokes' law applied.
questions.answer: Viscous drag = 2.2 x 10^-4 N.
steps: Terminal velocity v = distance / time = 0.45 / 7.3 = 0.0616 m s-1.
Stokes' law: F = 6 pi eta r v.

questions.question: A second sphere with a greater diameter but the same density is used in the same oil at the same temperature. Explain how the time to fall 0.45 m at terminal velocity compares with the original sphere.
questions.answer: The second sphere has a shorter time, because its terminal velocity is greater (v is proportional to r^2), so it covers 0.45 m in less time.
steps: At terminal velocity weight minus upthrust equals 6 pi eta r v, giving v proportional to r^2 when density and liquid are unchanged.
A greater diameter means a greater radius, so the terminal velocity is greater.
The time to fall 0.45 m is distance / v, so the time is shorter for the larger sphere.

questions.question: A student uses the falling-ball method on vegetable oil. Give one other measurement needed to determine the viscosity of the oil, in addition to the diameter, the time and the 20.0 cm fall distance.
questions.answer: The density of the oil (together with the density of the ball-bearing), which are needed to find the weight and upthrust and so the drag.
steps: Viscosity is found from Stokes' law, F = 6 pi eta r v, so the drag F must be known.
The drag at terminal velocity is weight minus upthrust, which needs the densities of the ball and oil.
So the density of the oil (and of the ball-bearing) is the additional measurement needed.

questions.question: The ball-bearing has diameter 1.24 mm and falls 20.0 cm in 1.3 s. The viscous drag is 5.6 x 10^-5 N. Calculate the viscosity of the oil.
questions.answer: Viscosity = 0.031 Pa s.
steps: Terminal velocity v = 0.200 / 1.3 = 0.154 m s-1.
Stokes' law: eta = F / (6 pi r v) = 5.6 x 10^-5 / (6 pi x 6.2 x 10^-4 x 0.154).

questions.question: The student repeats the experiment using the same oil at a lower temperature. Explain how this affects the time taken for the ball-bearing to fall 20.0 cm.
questions.answer: At lower temperature the oil is more viscous, so the drag is greater at a given speed, the terminal velocity is lower, and the ball takes longer to fall 20.0 cm.
steps: Viscosity increases as temperature decreases.
A larger viscosity gives a larger viscous drag at any given speed.
The terminal velocity is reached at a lower speed, since v is inversely proportional to viscosity.
A lower speed means the 20.0 cm fall takes a longer time.
